eabe302d54: The hills matter in later history too. They hold sites sacred to the Mwari (Mwali) shrine tradition, the grave of the Ndebele king Mzilikazi, and World’s View, where Cecil Rhodes is buried. A good guide explains these sites in full context, not as a colonial postcard.

c9b93b211d: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a powerful state on the southern African plateau. It was built and occupied roughly between the 11th and 15th centuries by ancestors of the Shona. Its walls are made of shaped granite blocks laid without mortar. The largest, around the Great Enclosure, are over 10 metres high in places. “Zimbabwe” is usually explained as coming from Shona words for “houses of stone”.
1c2c4a355f: Colonial-era writers refused to credit the site to African builders, and that falsehood shaped how it was presented for decades. Visiting with a guide who knows the archaeology and the politics of its interpretation is the point of coming.

ece291b684: Gonarezhou is managed in partnership with a conservation trust and forms part of the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park. It has fewer camps and far fewer visitors than the northern parks. The elephants have a history of poaching and can be wary, which is one more reason to go with an experienced guide.

d60eb31b9b: The Eastern Highlands run north to south along the border with Mozambique. In Nyanga, Mount Nyangani is the highest point in Zimbabwe at about 2,590 metres. There are trout streams, old terraced hill farms and Mtarazi Falls. Further south, the Bvumba near Mutare is misty forest and botanical gardens. Chimanimani has rugged quartzite peaks for multi-day hikes.
d6b24d354b: Few safari itineraries come here, which is the appeal. It suits walkers, birders after forest species, and anyone who wants cool nights and long views after time in the hot lowveld.

815624392b: Victoria Falls month by month · Mosi Travel
d1b2080106: In April spray hides much of the falls. In November parts of the lip are bare rock. This guide shows what you can actually see each month, and which side of the border to see it from.
6168737dca: High water, roughly March to May: the most water and the most spray. The falls are loud and you will get soaked. Often you see spray rather than water. Best seen from the air, or with patience on a breezy day.
94cea8bc07: Low water, roughly October to November: the least water. The Zambian side can be almost dry. The Zimbabwe side keeps a flow at the Main Falls and Devil’s Cataract, and you can see the whole basalt face and gorge.
6b331ae3b1: In between, June to August is the best balance for many people: plenty of water, much less spray. December to February the river rises again after the rains.
1d7146fcc0: Which side? Most of the falls’ width is on the Zimbabwe side, and the Zimbabwe path faces the falls along their length. That makes Zimbabwe the better side for most of the year. Zambia is at its best when the Eastern Cataract is flowing, and for experiences you can only have there: the Knife-Edge Bridge and, at low water, Livingstone Island.
5ab6a32895: How much water goes over, through the year
1ab6fe28bd: Relative flow, 0 (lowest) to 10 (peak). The usual shape of the year, not a measurement; real levels vary year to year.
af951dbb91: Victoria Falls by month: relative flow, spray, view and better side
8ba8cce65e: The river is rising after the first rains upstream. The Zimbabwe side has a full curtain at Devil’s Cataract and the Main Falls. On the Zambian side, the Eastern Cataract is only starting to fill.
882f6890ba: Livingstone Island trips usually stop around now as the water rises. Rafting usually still runs. Hot, humid, afternoon storms.
f9015869de: Water is building fast and the falls look full along most of their length, with spray not yet thick enough to hide them. Both sides are good: Zambia’s Eastern Cataract is flowing again.
44b272a062: A good compromise month: big water you can still see. Rains continue. Rafting may be cut short as levels climb.
c227d6ff01: High water. The spray cloud rises well above the gorge and drifts across the viewpoints, so views come and go with the wind. You will get wet on either side.
2b68b55530: Take a waterproof jacket, or accept you will be soaked. The Zimbabwe side’s long run of viewpoints gives you more chances to catch a clear moment. Rafting usually closes for high water around now.
ce376e92e6: Usually the peak. The column of spray can be seen from many kilometres away. Up close, much of the face is hidden behind spray, and some viewpoints show only white.
02a6c27a0c: For the scale of it, see it from the air (helicopter or microlight) or from further back. Around the full moon the park may open in the evening for the lunar rainbow. The Knife-Edge Bridge in Zambia is a drenching.
bf33d9dd25: Still in heavy flood, with dense spray. The rains have stopped, so the skies are clearer, and the spray on the Zimbabwe side keeps the rainforest dripping.
798dc937d9: Lunar rainbows are often at their best around now. Views through the spray are better in the early morning, before the wind picks up.
1e4bcaa2af: The flow is falling, but it is still a wall of water. More of the face shows as the spray thins, especially from mid-month.
670c42767e: Cool, dry and clear. A good month to combine the falls with Hwange or Mana Pools, which are drying out and getting better for game.
e409612953: For many people the best balance: a full curtain of water along most of the lip, with spray low enough that you can see the gorge and the rock below.
8c6a7ace62: Busy with school-holiday travellers from some markets; go to the rainforest at opening time. Rafting often reopens on the low-water run around now.
ce3d3db290: Very clear views. On the Zambian side the Eastern Cataract is thinning to separate streams. The Zimbabwe side still has strong flow at the Main Falls and Devil’s Cataract.
6e69a7e4ed: Livingstone Island and Devil’s Pool trips in Zambia usually start as the water drops, often from around mid-August. The full run of rapids is usually open for rafting.
0a3ff82c64: Low water. Much of the Zambian lip is bare basalt with a few streams. The Zimbabwe side keeps the main flow, so you see real water and the full depth of the gorge.
c7b4e21cce: Excellent for photographers who want the geology. Getting warm. The best months for game in Hwange and Mana Pools, so a strong time to combine.
5b04f18927: Near the lowest. The Zambian side can be almost dry. On the Zimbabwe side the Main Falls and Devil’s Cataract still run, though much thinner than in flood, and you can see the rock face along its length.
fc23180923: Very hot. Zimbabwe side clearly better for water. Fewer people at the falls; peak season in the national parks.
c02dd61028: Usually the lowest water of the year. The falls are separate streams over a long dark cliff. Some visitors are disappointed; others find the bare gorge more striking than the curtain.
125a6cdc09: Hot, with the first storms. Go for the gorge, the rafting and the town’s quiet. Combine with something else rather than come for the falls alone.
e9c67e593a: The local rains have started, but the river is slow to respond: most of the water comes from far upstream. Low flow, green surroundings.
fb56de0b8d: Holiday-season busy around Christmas. The Zimbabwe side remains the one to see. Devil’s Pool may still be running early in the month, depending on levels.

6e1afa568a: Why Zimbabwe guides: walking and canoe safaris · Mosi Travel
060c17ca77: A fully licensed professional guide in Zimbabwe has spent years on foot with dangerous game and passed some of the hardest practical exams in the safari world. That is why we build trips around them.
da18a2b371: In Zimbabwe, leading guests on foot among big game is licensed work. The Professional Guide licence is issued by the national parks authority (Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority), after a long apprenticeship and a series of written, firearms and field exams.
18b2df3743: Many countries use shorter courses or written qualifications. The Zimbabwean system is built around practical assessment. Senior guides and examiners watch candidates in the field, on foot, around elephant, buffalo and lion, and judge how they read the animals and keep a group safe. Many candidates take years to pass, and some never do.
a0f9527b50: The industry body, the Zimbabwe Professional Guides Association, represents licensed guides.
5a05824436: Pass written exams on ecology, animal behaviour, plants, birds, history, law and safety to register as a learner professional guide.
ccdd949e4f: Years of work under licensed guides, logging time on foot and with dangerous game, and building up a record signed off by mentors.
036c5ee2ac: Shooting proficiency with a heavy-calibre rifle under pressure. Guides carry one on every walk and almost never use it.

7f00e4d5c9: In defence of Victoria Falls at low water · Mosi Travel
c35129550d: Every year someone arrives at Victoria Falls in October or November, looks across from the Zimbabwe side and feels a bit cheated. The brochure showed a solid wall of white water. What they see is a long cliff of dark basalt with separate streams pouring off it, and on the Zambian side, in places, nothing much at all.
d250ba4971: That is the river doing what it always does. The Zambezi’s flow at the falls follows rain that falls far upstream months earlier. It usually peaks around April and drops to its lowest around November. Peak flow in a typical year is many times the low-water flow.
38859420e8: What you see when the water drops
f07ebd63f7: At high water the spray hides most of the falls. At low water you see their structure: the zigzag of gorges cut back into the basalt as the falls retreated upstream over a very long time, the islands on the lip, the dark rock face. With a guide who knows the geology, the low-water falls explain themselves in a way the flood never does.
de6d4697de: The Zimbabwe side still carries real water through the dry months, mainly at the Main Falls and Devil’s Cataract. That is why our month-by-month guide points you to Zimbabwe from about September to January.
e185851758: Why we often recommend it anyway
effab59543: It fits the best safari months. September and October are when game in Hwange and Mana Pools is most concentrated around water. Pairing the two is easy.
d862775c5a: The rafting is at its best. Low water usually means the full run of rapids below the falls is open.
7d4f773faa: Fewer people at the viewpoints. Most visitors to the falls come when the water is higher.
6ab3be3507: If seeing the falls in full flood matters most to you, come between March and July and accept the spray. If you would rather understand them, low water has a lot going for it.
e0ecb95576: What to pack for a walking safari · Mosi Travel
d54b372e00: Walking with a professional guide changes what you need. You are on the ground with animals that can see, hear and smell you, so what you wear and carry matters more than on a game drive. Your camp will send its own list. These are the points guides raise most often.
41c6edc9c5: Muted colours: khaki, olive, brown, grey. Avoid white and bright colours, which stand out a long way in the bush. Many guides also ask you to avoid dark blue and black in tsetse areas, because they attract the flies.
e47b00a78f: Long, light trousers against grass seeds, thorns and ticks. Shorts are fine on some walks; ask your guide.
a08fb0720d: Layers for early starts. June to August mornings can be close to freezing in Hwange and Matobo before the sun is up.
e07e01b97f: A wide-brimmed hat that will not blow off.
21ef39b7d7: Comfortable, broken-in walking shoes or light boots with quiet soles. Heavy mountain boots are unnecessary on most safari walks and noisy on dry leaves. In Mana Pools and on sand rivers you will walk on soft ground for hours, so comfort matters more than ankle support.
f32263c10e: Binoculars: one pair each if you can. You will use them more on foot than in a vehicle.
c5a5362898: A water bottle, and a small daypack that does not rustle.
71124f8a09: Any medication you need, carried yourself rather than left in camp.
482e7dfd90: Anything noisy, perfume, and the urge to talk. The best walks are mostly quiet, with the guide stopping to show you what is on the ground. Our page on how Zimbabwe’s guides are trained explains how a walk is run and why the briefing at the start matters.
353c65aafd: The walls of Great Zimbabwe are the largest ancient stone structures in Africa south of the Sahara. They were built without mortar from granite split into regular blocks. The city at its height may have held many thousands of people. The country takes its name from the site.
000905010d: Archaeologists agree that Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona-speaking people who live in the region today, from around the 11th century. It flourished in the 13th to 15th centuries as the centre of a state whose wealth came from cattle, gold and long-distance trade reaching the Indian Ocean coast. Glass beads and Chinese and Persian ceramics found at the site show how far those connections went.
14dc334d00: For much of the colonial period, European writers and the Rhodesian state promoted the idea that the city must have been built by outsiders, anyone but Africans. Archaeologists rejected these claims early in the twentieth century. The myth lasted because it was politically useful, and parts of the site were damaged by early treasure-seekers and careless digging.
4de1a3d64b: Knowing this changes how you walk the site. The guide’s job here is not only to point at walls. It is to explain how the site has been read, misread and reclaimed, including in the independence struggle, when the name Zimbabwe was chosen for the new country.
7e5d02f65c: Go early. The light is better and the climb to the Hill Complex is cooler.
21dde6dd1e: Start at the top. The Hill Complex is the oldest part, and from it you look down on the Great Enclosure and the valley.
c6bfd0d846: Leave time for the museum, where several of the soapstone Zimbabwe Birds are displayed.
06506d4912: Stay nearby. A night at Lake Mutirikwi means you are not driving in the heat of the day.
